Reference: Ericson and Pakes (1995)

Model Setting

The paper builds a general model of firm and industry dynamics with entry, exit and firm-specific uncertainty, intended as a framework for empirical work. Firm-level panels show simultaneous entry and exit, very different outcome paths for firms that start from similar conditions, and industry structures that never remain stable. Earlier models either let firms passively learn a fixed type (Jovanovic 1982), assume a continuum of price-taking firms hit by exogenous shocks (Hopenhayn 1992), or restrict attention to duopoly with specific functional forms. Here a finite number of heterogeneous firms invest in a research and exploration process whose outcome is random, compete in a spot market, and may exit; potential entrants pay a sunk cost to come in. Idiosyncratic investment outcomes, the success of rivals, and competitive pressure from outside the industry move each firm's state up or down, and a long enough run of bad outcomes makes it optimal to liquidate, so that exit and selection are endogenous.

The paper has four results. First, each incumbent's dynamic problem has a unique bounded value function, a unique investment policy and a cutoff exit policy; firms invest only on a bounded set of states and every firm dies in finite time with probability one. Second, the value of being in the industry falls to the scrap value as the number of active firms grows, so the number of entrants and the number of active firms are bounded and the state space is finite. Third, a rational expectations Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium in investment, entry and exit strategies exists. Fourth, the equilibrium process for the industry structure is ergodic: there is a unique positive recurrent class of structures and a unique invariant distribution to which the distribution of structures converges from any initial condition, so the industry never settles on a limit structure. A Cournot example computed with the algorithm of Pakes and McGuire (1994) illustrates the finer properties, which depend on functional forms. The note on Pakes and McGuire (1994) covers the algorithm and the differentiated-product example; this note states the general framework and its theory.

In equilibrium all firms optimize against the distribution Q(⋅∣s)Q(\cdot|s)Q(⋅∣s) of future structures, and their decisions generate exactly that distribution. Because strategies depend only on the payoff-relevant state (ω,s)(\omega,s)(ω,s) and each firm takes the distribution of others' outcomes as given, the equilibrium is a Markov-perfect Nash equilibrium in the sense of Maskin and Tirole (1988): each policy remains optimal at every state, however that state was reached. The equilibrium generates a time-homogeneous Markov process (S,Q(⋅∣⋅),s0)(S,Q(\cdot|\cdot),s^0)(S,Q(⋅∣⋅),s0) on industry structures, together with the sequences of entrants mt=m(st)m_t=m(s_t)mt​=m(st​), of highest exit states, and of numbers of exiting firms. Within a period all decisions are simultaneous.

Proposition 1: Optimal Incumbent Behaviour

Under assumptions A.0 to A.7, Proposition 1 has three parts. (a) There is a unique value function V(ω,s)V(\omega,s)V(ω,s), monotonically increasing in ω\omegaω, uniformly bounded and satisfying the Bellman equation; a unique optimal investment policy with x(ω,s)≤xˉ<∞x(\omega,s)\leq\bar{x}<\inftyx(ω,s)≤xˉ<∞; and an optimal termination policy χ(ω,s)∈{0,1}\chi(\omega,s)\in\{0,1\}χ(ω,s)∈{0,1}. The proposition describes a life cycle. In the upper coasting states CuC_uCu​ the firm earns profits from past success and does not invest, because the bounded value function is too flat to cover the marginal cost of investment. In the lower coasting states ClC_lCl​ the firm neither invests nor exits; it may even shut down production (a mothballed plant) and forgo the scrap value in the hope that the structure improves. Without such an improvement its state drifts down into LLL. Proposition 2: Bounding the Number of Firms

Finite lifetimes do not by themselves bound the industry, since entry could exceed exit forever. If VVV were decreasing in sss under the pre-order, entry would choke itself off, but interactions among firms (entry deterrence in particular) mean that VVV is not in general monotone in sss. Existence of Equilibrium

Proposition 3 states that under assumptions A.0 to A.5, assumption A.6 holds when Q(⋅∣⋅)Q(\cdot|\cdot)Q(⋅∣⋅) is built from the multinomial formula and the beliefs qω(s^′∣s)q_\omega(\hat{s}'|s)qω​(s^′∣s) are its marginals; its proof is only in the working paper version, Ericson and Pakes (1992). Assumptions A.6 and A.7 are therefore consequences of the basic assumptions. Theorem 1: under assumptions A.0 to A.5 an equilibrium satisfying conditions (a) to (e) exists. The proof is a fixed-point argument. Let L∈(ΔS)S\mathcal{L}\in(\Delta^S)^SL∈(ΔS)S denote the collection of conditional distributions generated by a kernel QQQ, where ΔS\Delta^SΔS is the simplex of probability measures on the finite set SSS. A map ζ\zetaζ takes a transition function into the value function, investment policy and entry value that solve the Bellman equation and the entry equation; a map ψ\psiψ takes these into the transition function they generate through the multinomial formula:

Ψ≡ψ∘ζ:(ΔS)S→(ΔS)S,L∗=Ψ(L∗)(22)\Psi\equiv\psi\circ\zeta:(\Delta^S)^S\to(\Delta^S)^S,\qquad\mathcal{L}^*=\Psi(\mathcal{L}^*) \tag{22}Ψ≡ψ∘ζ:(ΔS)S→(ΔS)S,L∗=Ψ(L∗)(22)

Both maps are continuous (lemmas whose proofs are again in the working paper), and (ΔS)S(\Delta^S)^S(ΔS)S is convex and compact, so Brouwer's fixed point theorem gives a rationally anticipated transition function L∗\mathcal{L}^*L∗. The theorem asserts existence only; uniqueness is not claimed. The equilibrium has stationary values, policies and transition probabilities, but the sequence of states of any firm and the sequence of structures of the industry are random.

The substance of the proof is the uniqueness of the recurrent class. A recurrent class exists because SSS is finite. Implications of Ergodicity

First, there is never a limit structure. All structures in RRR are realized infinitely often, and the structure next period is only probabilistically related to the current one, so the link between structure and behaviour, and between structure and welfare, is weaker than in traditional models. All firms die, but entrants replenish the industry, which lives forever. Second, a stochastic regularity appears. From a transient initial structure the industry reaches RRR in finite time, and afterwards the share of time spent in each structure approaches its invariant probability:

lim⁡T→∞1T∑Is=μs∗(27)\lim_{T\to\infty}\frac{1}{T}\sum I_s=\mu^*_s \tag{27}T→∞lim​T1​∑Is​=μs∗​(27)

where IsI_sIs​ indicates that the structure is sss. Time averages approximate the ergodic distribution, whose mass shows which structures are natural for the industry given the primitives. Third, the influence of the initial condition fades: two histories with different initial structures have identical distributions over future paths once they meet, which happens with probability one. For policy analysis the natural object is therefore the effect of a change in primitives on the recurrent class, the invariant distribution and the transition into the class. At the firm level, the equilibrium is characterized by flux: firms that make identical investments have different outcomes, rank reversals in sales or profits occur repeatedly within a cohort, entry and exit can be simultaneous (the exit bound lies below the entry states), and the common shock makes firms' outcomes positively correlated.

The paper compares these properties with other models. Competitive models have a continuum of infinitesimal firms and a deterministic limit structure. In Jovanovic (1982) each firm learns a time-invariant parameter; in the limit there is no entry or exit and a fixed distribution of surviving firms, and the model is not ergodic, because the fixed parameter differentiates firms forever. In Hopenhayn (1992) the fixed limiting distribution incorporates entry, exit and changing productivities due to exogenous shocks, and the model is ergodic. The present model is also ergodic, but with a finite number of firms, so the structure itself stays random. A nonparametric test based on a mixing condition can distinguish ergodic from non-ergodic models (Pakes and Ericson 1990). Game-theoretic duopoly models mostly generate a deterministic evolution to a fixed structure; none combines an endogenous structure, finitely lived heterogeneous firms, and endogenous entry and exit. The framework also suggests nonparametric corrections for selection and simultaneity (Olley and Pakes), and has been applied to mergers, hospitals and productivity in telecommunications equipment.

Numerical Example

The example is a homogeneous-product industry with Cournot competition in the spot market. Marginal cost is θω=γe−ω\theta_\omega=\gamma e^{-\omega}θω​=γe−ω, inverse demand is p(Q)=D−Qp(Q)=D-Qp(Q)=D−Q and fff is a fixed cost. With ω∗\omega^*ω∗ the lowest state of a firm that produces and ∣s∗∣=∑k≥ω∗sk|s^*|=\sum_{k\geq\omega^*}s_k∣s∗∣=∑k≥ω∗​sk​ the number of producing firms, profits are:

The paper prints the maximum outside the square, as the larger of the squared margin minus fff and −f-f−f, which never binds; it is placed inside the square here. A firm with A(ω,s)=−fA(\omega,s)=-fA(ω,s)=−f is not active in the spot market but may remain in the industry. The transition is specified by:

with cω=cc_\omega=ccω​=c, at most one entrant per period (x1e=xex^e_1=x^ex1e​=xe and xme=∞x^e_m=\inftyxme​=∞ for m>1m>1m>1), and entry at ωe=ω0+η\omega^e=\omega^0+\etaωe=ω0+η. Here τ\tauτ is the increment in the log of the firm's efficiency and −η-\eta−η the increment in the log of a factor price index. The parameter values are D=4D=4D=4, f=0.2f=0.2f=0.2, xe=0.4x^e=0.4xe=0.4, ω0=4\omega^0=4ω0=4, ϕ=0.2\phi=0.2ϕ=0.2, c=1c=1c=1, δ=0.7\delta=0.7δ=0.7, a=3a=3a=3 and β=0.925\beta=0.925β=0.925 (the table note prints the value 0.7 under the symbol SSS). The Markov-perfect Nash (MPN) equilibrium is compared with a colluder (a multi-plant monopolist that maximizes total profits) and a social planner, each simulated from one firm at the entry state.

  • Structure: over 10,000 periods the MPN industry has one active firm in 27.9 percent of periods, two in 70.8 percent, three in 1.2 percent and four in 0.1 percent; the colluder has one firm in 92.4 percent and the planner in 98.3 percent. Periods with both entry and exit are 16.5 percent (MPN), 5.4 percent (colluder) and 1.2 percent (planner); the entry rate is 0.19, 0.08 and 0.02. Entry and exit are positively correlated.

  • Prices and investment: average price is 1.79 under MPN and 2.22 under collusion; average total investment is 1.05, 0.68 and 0.84 (planner). The colluder and the planner internalize the cash flow that entry and investment take from other incumbents, and so have less of both.

  • Welfare: over 100 runs of 100 periods, discounted consumer benefits are 27.4 (MPN) and 6.6 (colluder), net cash flow 11.6 and 22.5, entry-exit fees 2.5 and 1.0, and total welfare 36.5 (standard deviation 11.9), 28.1 (14.1) and 58.8 for the planner. The colluder's structure resembles the planner's, but MPN welfare is much closer to the planner's; still, the gap is on the order of 40 percent, against 2 to 3 percent in the differentiated-product example. The difference between MPN and colluder welfare is smaller than the standard deviation of either.

  • Investment policy and life cycle: investment is first increasing and then decreasing in the firm's own state, because the bounded value function is convex and then concave. Entrants start with low investment, so most never overcome the negative drift and die young; the few with good early draws invest more and tend to stay productive for a long time. Mortality is therefore high in an initial period, and the distributions of lifetimes and realized values are very skewed. With a weak rival, a firm's investment surges again at ω=8\omega=8ω=8 in order to deter entry (a potential entrant enters against one firm at ω=7\omega=7ω=7 but not against one firm at ω=9\omega=9ω=9), which shows why the value function need not be monotone in sss. A sufficiently efficient firm deters entry, yet even the most efficient firm eventually decays.

This is the per-period payoff of an incumbent that stays in the industry. A(ω,s)A(\omega,s)A(ω,s) is the profit from the spot market, a reduced form that already embodies the static equilibrium (prices or quantities) among the firms listed in sss; it depends on the firm's own efficiency ω\omegaω and on the whole counting measure sss, which includes the firm itself. x≥0x\geq0x≥0 is the amount of investment activity and c(ω)≥c‾>0c(\omega)\geq\underline{c}>0c(ω)≥c​>0 its unit cost, so c(ω)⋅xc(\omega)\cdot xc(ω)⋅x is the expenditure on research and exploration. Both terms are in the same money units per period.

The functional form is linear in xxx. This puts all the curvature of the investment problem into the transition probabilities π(⋅∣ω,x)\pi(\cdot|\omega,x)π(⋅∣ω,x) of equation (3), which are assumed concave in xxx at the higher states, and it makes the marginal cost of investment the constant c(ω)c(\omega)c(ω) that appears in the first-order condition (8) and in the comparison (16). The lower bound c‾>0\underline{c}>0c​>0 matters: because the marginal gain from investment vanishes where the value function is flat, equation (17), a marginal cost bounded away from zero is what switches investment off at very high and very low states.

Investment does not enter AAA, so it has no current benefit; it only shifts the distribution of next period's state. RRR can be negative: a firm may run losses, or pay for investment out of negative profits, when the option value of staying is high enough. RRR is the flow term of the sequential problem (5) and of the Bellman equation (6).

These are the limit conditions of assumption A.3 on the reduced-form profit function. The first says that profits are bounded above: however efficient the firm becomes, A(ω,s)A(\omega,s)A(ω,s) converges to a finite Aˉ\bar{A}Aˉ. Together with β<1\beta<1β<1 this bounds the value function by Vˉ≤Aˉ/(1−β)\bar{V}\leq\bar{A}/(1-\beta)Vˉ≤Aˉ/(1−β), and a bounded monotone value function must become flat, which is what stops investment at high states in equation (17).

The second says that a firm whose state falls far enough earns less than (1−β)ϕ(1-\beta)\phi(1−β)ϕ whatever the structure sss. The number (1−β)ϕ(1-\beta)\phi(1−β)ϕ is the per-period annuity equivalent of the scrap value: a perpetual flow of (1−β)ϕ(1-\beta)\phi(1−β)ϕ is worth ϕ\phiϕ at the start of a period. A firm that earns less than this forever would rather take ϕ\phiϕ now, and this drives the exit bound derived from equation (18).

The third line is the crowding condition. S^n(ω)\hat{S}_n(\omega)S^n​(ω) is the set of structures in which at least nnn firms (the firm itself included) are at states no lower than ω\omegaω. With that many equally or more efficient firms, profit can exceed the annuity value of scrap only by a remainder that vanishes as nnn grows. It is used in the form of equation (20) to prove Proposition 2, equation (19).

The remainder is printed as o(1/n)o(1/n)o(1/n) in the paper. The proof of Proposition 2 only uses that the remainder, called θ(n)\theta(n)θ(n) in equation (20), is monotone and tends to zero, so the rate is not essential. A Cournot example: with nnn identical firms, linear demand and no fixed cost, profit per firm is of order 1/(n+1)21/(n+1)^21/(n+1)2, which is indeed o(1/n)o(1/n)o(1/n).

This is the incumbent's sequential problem. The controls are, for every future date τ≥t\tau\geq tτ≥t, an investment xτ≥0x_\tau\geq0xτ​≥0 and a continuation indicator χτ∈{0,1}\chi_\tau\in\{0,1\}χτ​∈{0,1}; exit is permanent, so χτ=0\chi_\tau=0χτ​=0 implies χσ=0\chi_\sigma=0χσ​=0 for all later σ\sigmaσ. The outer maximum with ϕ\phiϕ lets the firm exit immediately at ttt.

The expectation is over the firm's own controlled process p(ω′∣ω,x)p(\omega'|\omega,x)p(ω′∣ω,x) of equation (3) and over the perceived kernel qω(s^′∣s)q_\omega(\hat{s}'|s)qω​(s^′∣s) for its competitors. Rivals' investments are not observed, so policies can depend only on the history of states.

The equation summarizes Proposition 1(b): investment is zero outside a bounded band of states, and exit follows a cutoff. Both parts follow from the monotonicity and boundedness of VVV in Proposition 1(a).

No investment at the extremes. ω‾‾(s)≡max⁡{ω ∣ V(ω,s)=ϕ}\underline{\underline{\omega}}(s)\equiv\max\{\omega\ |\ V(\omega,s)=\phi\}ω​​(s)≡max{ω ∣ V(ω,s)=ϕ}

makes χ(ω,s)=0\chi(\omega,s)=0χ(ω,s)=0 if and only if ω≤ω‾‾(s)\omega\leq\underline{\underline{\omega}}(s)ω≤ω​​(s). T(ω0,s0)T(\omega_0,s_0)T(ω0​,s0​) is the firm's lifetime: the first date at which the state (ωt,st)(\omega_t,s_t)(ωt​,st​), generated by the optimal policies and the equilibrium kernel from the initial state (ω0,s0)(\omega_0,s_0)(ω0​,s0​), enters the liquidation set LLL of equation (14). It is a stopping time, since whether T≤tT\leq tT≤t is known from the history up to ttt, and it is the date at which χ\chiχ first equals zero. The condition "(ω0,s0)=(ω0,s0)(\omega_0,s_0)=(\omega_0,s_0)(ω0​,s0​)=(ω0​,s0​)" inside the braces is printed this way in the paper; it is a tautology and only records that the path starts at the given initial state. A cleaner statement is

T(ω0,s0)=inf⁡{t≥0 ∣ (ωt,st)∈L}for the path started at (ω0,s0).T(\omega_0,s_0)=\inf\{t\geq0\ |\ (\omega_t,s_t)\in L\}\quad\text{for the path started at }(\omega_0,s_0).T(ω0​,s0​)=inf{t≥0 ∣ (ωt​,st​)∈L}for the path started at (ω0​,s0​).

Proposition 1(c) says two things about it. First, T<∞T<\inftyT<∞ with probability one: every firm dies. The reason is that the set of states a firm can occupy is finite (equation (14) and the remark after it) and from any of them there is a run of bad luck of bounded length, the outside alternative advancing while the firm's investment fails in each period, that carries the firm into LLL. If such a run of length at most ℓ\ellℓ has probability at least ρ>0\rho>0ρ>0 from every state, then

Pr⁡{T>nℓ}≤(1−ρ)n→0,\Pr\{T>n\ell\}\leq(1-\rho)^n\to0,Pr{T>nℓ}≤(1−ρ)n→0,

so TTT is finite almost surely and even has a finite mean. This uses pη>0p_\eta>0pη​>0 for some η<0\eta<0η<0 and a positive probability of failure, π(ω∣ω,x)>0\pi(\omega|\omega,x)>0π(ω∣ω,x)>0. Second, TTT is stochastically increasing in ω0\omega_0ω0​: a firm that starts higher lives longer in the sense of first-order stochastic dominance. The paper proves this by coupling two paths that start at ω1<ω2\omega_1<\omega_2ω1​<ω2​ and letting them coincide after they first meet. The result underlies the life-cycle and selection interpretation, and it is why the industry needs continual entry, equation (23), to survive.

Unique recurrent class. A finite chain has at least one recurrent class, and every recurrent class is closed. Since sˉ\bar{s}sˉ is reachable from every structure, it is reachable from inside any recurrent class and therefore belongs to it. Two distinct classes are disjoint, so there is exactly one, RRR, and all structures outside RRR are transient. In a finite chain recurrence is positive recurrence: the expected return time mQ(s,s)mQ(s,s)mQ(s,s) is finite for s∈Rs\in Rs∈R.
